result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Is It Really a Straight Line?" subtitle: "Checking linearity · polynomials · categorising · transformations · U-shapes hidden by a linear term · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - Regression workshop: every continuous predictor entered as a **straight line** - Today: **how to see** that the line is wrong, and the **simple** fixes - By the end you can: - use **residual plots and smoothers** to detect curvature - fit **polynomial** and **log** terms - explain what **categorising** costs - see how a **linear term can hide a U-shape** ::: ## Our data: an NCD risk-factor survey ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="55%"} - **4,000 adults** aged 18 to 80 (synthetic) - **SBP** (mmHg) and **10-year CVD event** (`cvd10`, 10% had one) - Age, BMI, salt (g/day), activity (hours/week), sex, smoking - Questions: does SBP rise **evenly** with age? Does CVD risk rise **steadily** with BMI? ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncd |> select(age, sex, bmi, salt, activity, smoker, sbp, cvd10) |> head(6) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 8 age sex bmi salt activity smoker sbp cvd10 1 66 Male 25.4 12.4 3.5 0 130 0 2 23 Male 25.3 8.5 4.7 0 127 0 3 49 Male 27 10.2 3.6 1 126 0 4 43 Male 18.6 6.4 3.6 1 99 0 5 34 Male 23.3 9.7 5.4 1 116 0 6 36 Male 23.9 8.2 2 0 94 0 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — Seeing curvature {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Straight line vs smoother ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(ncd, aes(age, sbp)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.12) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", colour = col_red, se = FALSE) + geom_smooth(method = "loess", colour = col_blue, se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x) + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "SBP (mmHg)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_beyond_linear_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.key} The **red** line says "the same rise per year at every age". The **blue** loess smoother shows SBP rising **slowly until about 45 and faster after**. ::: ## Residuals against the predictor ::: {.cell output-location='slide'} ```{.r .cell-code} m_lin <- lm(sbp ~ age + bmi + salt + activity + sex + smoker, data = ncd) ggplot(data.frame(age = ncd$age, res = resid(m_lin)), aes(age, res)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.12) + geom_smooth(se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, method = "loess") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = 2) + labs(y = "Residual") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_beyond_linear_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=900} ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - If the straight line were right, the smoother would be **flat at 0** - It curves: **negative at both ends and positive in the middle** - Do this for **every continuous predictor** in a model ::: # Topic 2 — Simple fixes {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Polynomial terms ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_quad <- lm(sbp ~ poly(age, 2) + bmi + salt + activity + sex + smoker, data = ncd) anova(m_lin, m_quad) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: sbp ~ age + bmi + salt + activity + sex + smoker Model 2: sbp ~ poly(age, 2) + bmi + salt + activity + sex + smoker Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 3993 511350 2 3992 506767 1 4583 36.102 2.039e-09 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(linear = AIC(m_lin), quadratic = AIC(m_quad)) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` linear quadratic 30771 30737 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.incremental} - Adding **age²** improves the fit (F test p ≈ 2×10⁻⁹; AIC down by about **34**) - `poly(age, 2)`: **orthogonal** terms; `age + I(age^2)`: raw terms - Polynomial coefficients are **hard to read**: look at the **curve**; they misbehave at the **ends** ::: ## Categorising the predictor ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ncd <- ncd |> mutate(age_grp = cut(age, c(0, 29, 44, 59, 100), labels = c("<30", "30-44", "45-59", "60+"))) m_cat <- lm(sbp ~ age_grp + bmi + salt + activity + sex + smoker, data = ncd) c(linear = AIC(m_lin), quadratic = AIC(m_quad), four_groups = AIC(m_cat)) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` linear quadratic four_groups 30771 30737 30810 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} The four age groups fit **worse than a straight line** (AIC 30,810). Categorising **throws away** the variation within a group, forces **steps** at arbitrary cut-points, loses **power**, and hides the shape. Use groups to **describe** (a table), not to **model**. ::: ## Transformations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_log <- lm(sbp ~ age + bmi + salt + log1p(activity) + sex + smoker, data = ncd) c(linear = AIC(m_lin), log_activity = AIC(m_log)) |> round(0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` linear log_activity 30771 30750 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} Activity shows **diminishing returns**: the first hours of activity lower SBP most. **`log(1 + activity)`** captures it (AIC down by 21) with **no extra parameter**, and keeps a **single coefficient**. ::: # Topic 3 — A U-shape that a line cannot see {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## BMI and CVD risk: linear term ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g_lin <- glm(cvd10 ~ age + bmi + sex + smoker, data = ncd, family = binomial) round(exp(cbind(OR = coef(g_lin), confint.default(g_lin)))["bmi", ], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` OR 2.5 % 97.5 % 1.007 0.983 1.032 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} **OR 1.007** (95% CI 0.98 to 1.03): "BMI has **no effect**". That is **wrong**. ::: ## Add a quadratic term ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g_quad <- glm(cvd10 ~ age + bmi + I(bmi^2) + sex + smoker, data = ncd, family = binomial) anova(g_lin, g_quad, test = "Chisq") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Deviance Table Model 1: cvd10 ~ age + bmi + sex + smoker Model 2: cvd10 ~ age + bmi + I(bmi^2) + sex + smoker Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi) 1 3995 2271.9 2 3994 2041.0 1 230.89 < 2.2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} b <- coef(g_quad); -b[["bmi"]] / (2 * b[["I(bmi^2)"]]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 24.53069 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.key} The quadratic term is overwhelming (deviance drop **231**). Risk is **lowest near BMI 24.5** and rises **both** for low and high BMI. The straight line averaged the **two arms of the U** and found **nothing**. A model without a check for shape would have **missed a real effect**. ::: ## What to do ::: {.good} 1. **Plot** the outcome (or residuals) against each continuous predictor with a **smoother** 2. Try **transformations** (log) when returns **diminish** 3. Try **polynomial or spline** terms when the shape is **curved or bending** (Session 2) 4. **Do not categorise** unless the question is about groups 5. Compare with **AIC or a test**, and **plot** the result ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `curves-workshop/labs/lab1_linear.R` - curve vs straight line, residual smoother - quadratic, categorised and log versions - a U-shape in a logistic model and its turning point ::: **Time:** 35 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="k1h2l4.oikwc9" data-show="VGhlIHN0cmFpZ2h0LWxpbmUgdGVybSBmb3IgYWdlIGlzIHRoZSB3cm9uZyBzaGFwZSBmb3Ig dGhlIHJlbGF0aW9uc2hpcA==" data-explain="UmVzaWR1YWxzIHNob3VsZCBiZSBmbGF0IGFyb3VuZCB6ZXJvIGlmIHRoZSBmdW5jdGlvbmFs IGZvcm0gaXMgcmlnaHQuIEEgc3lzdGVtYXRpYyBjdXJ2ZSBtZWFucyB0aGUgbW9kZWwgaXMg bWlzLXNwZWNpZmllZCBmb3IgdGhhdCB2YXJpYWJsZS4="} A smoother through the residuals against age is a clear U-shape. What does this suggest? - The errors are not normal, so the outcome should be transformed in the model - Age has no effect on the outcome after the other variables are included - The straight-line term for age is the wrong shape for the relationship - The model needs more adults before the pattern can be interpreted ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="k1hftu.oilatn" data-show="SXQgZGlzY2FyZHMgaW5mb3JtYXRpb24gYW5kIGNyZWF0ZXMgYXJ0aWZpY2lhbCBqdW1wcyBh dCB0aGUgY3V0LXBvaW50cw==" data-explain="RXZlcnlvbmUgaW4gYSBncm91cCBpcyB0cmVhdGVkIGFsaWtlLCBzbyB2YXJpYXRpb24gd2l0 aGluIHRoZSBncm91cCBpcyBsb3N0LCBwb3dlciBmYWxscywgYW5kIHRoZSBjdXQtcG9pbnRz IGFyZSBhcmJpdHJhcnkuIEhlcmUgZm91ciBhZ2UgZ3JvdXBzIGZpdHRlZCB3b3JzZSB0aGFu IGEgbGluZS4="} Why is cutting a continuous variable into a few groups usually a poor idea? - It forces the relationship to be exactly linear within each of the groups - It makes the standard errors smaller than the true ones in the model - It cannot be used when the outcome is a yes or no variable - It discards information and creates artificial jumps at the cut-points ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="k1ht2g.oilpax" data-show="VGhlIHJpc2sgaXMgVS1zaGFwZWQsIGFuZCB0aGUgbGluZSBhdmVyYWdlcyB0aGUgdHdvIGFy bXMgdG8gbm90aGluZw==" data-explain="V2hlbiByaXNrIGZhbGxzIHRoZW4gcmlzZXMsIHRoZSBiZXN0IHN0cmFpZ2h0IGxpbmUgaXMg bmVhcmx5IGZsYXQuIEEgZmxleGlibGUgdGVybSByZXZlYWxzIHRoZSB0cnVlIHNoYXBlLCB3 aGljaCBhIGxpbmVhciB0ZXJtIGNhbiBoaWRlIGNvbXBsZXRlbHku"} In a logistic model the BMI odds ratio is 1.007 (CI 0.98 to 1.03), yet a squared BMI term is highly significant. What is the best interpretation? - The risk is U-shaped, and the line averages the two arms to nothing - BMI is unrelated to the outcome, and the squared term is a chance finding - The linear term is right, and the squared term just improves the p-value - The odds ratio must be wrong, because an effect so close to one is not credible ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="k1i6b6.oim3sb" data-show="UmVwbGFjZSBhY3Rpdml0eSBieSBsb2coMSArIGFjdGl2aXR5KQ==" data-explain="QSBsb2cgdHJhbnNmb3JtYXRpb24gZmxhdHRlbnMgdGhlIGN1cnZlIGFzIGFjdGl2aXR5IGdy b3dzLCB3aXRoIGEgc2luZ2xlIGNvZWZmaWNpZW50LiBUaGUgc3F1YXJlIHdvdWxkIGdpdmUg YWNjZWxlcmF0aW5nLCBub3QgZGltaW5pc2hpbmcsIHJldHVybnMu"} Activity lowers SBP with diminishing returns. Which simple change in the model captures this? - Replace activity by the square of activity - Replace activity by log(1 + activity) - Round activity to whole hours before the model is fitted - Divide activity by the age of each adult in the study ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="k1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="k1ijjx.oimi9q" data-show="VGhlIEJNSSBhdCB3aGljaCB0aGUgcHJlZGljdGVkIHJpc2sgaXMgbG93ZXN0" data-explain="VGhlIHZlcnRleCBvZiB0aGUgcGFyYWJvbGEgaXMgd2hlcmUgaXRzIHNsb3BlIGlzIHplcm8u IEZvciB0aGlzIFUtc2hhcGVkIHJpc2sgY3VydmUgaXQgaXMgdGhlIEJNSSB3aXRoIHRoZSBs b3dlc3QgcHJlZGljdGVkIHJpc2su"} A quadratic model for BMI has the turning point -b / (2c) at 24.5. What is this value? - The average BMI of the adults in the sample - The BMI at which the odds ratio equals one exactly - The BMI at which the squared term becomes significant - The BMI at which the predicted risk is lowest ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - **Plot** the outcome or residuals against each predictor with a **smoother** - A **linear term can hide** a U-shape (OR 1.007!) - **log** for diminishing returns; **polynomial** or **splines** for bends - **Do not categorise** to model; groups are for describing - Compare by **AIC or tests**, then **plot** ::: **Next:** Session 2: splines

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
